lesson_title: Nature of crimes: medieval and early modern
claim: The Witchcraft Act of 1563, passed under Elizabeth I, made witchcraft a capital offence for the first time in England.
issue: This is factually wrong on two counts. First, Henry VIII's Witchcraft Act of 1542 was the first English statute to make witchcraft a felony punishable by death (though it was repealed in 1547 by Edward VI). Second, the 1563 Act did NOT make all witchcraft a capital offence — it imposed the death penalty only for witchcraft causing death, and for second offences of lesser witchcraft. First offences causing injury (but not death) carried one year's imprisonment and pillory.
correction: The 1563 Witchcraft Act was NOT the first to make witchcraft capital in England; Henry VIII's 1542 Act had already done so (repealed 1547). The 1563 Act also did not make all witchcraft capital — only witchcraft resulting in death (and repeat lesser offences). A more accurate formulation: 'The Witchcraft Act of 1563, passed under Elizabeth I, brought witchcraft under secular criminal law and imposed the death penalty for cases where the victim died, reviving and extending the approach of the repealed 1542 Act.'

claim: The Metropolitan Police was established with approximately 3,200 officers organised on military lines
issue: The initial operational strength of the Metropolitan Police when it took to the streets on 29 September 1829 was approximately 1,000 officers (specifically: 2 Commissioners, 8 Superintendents, 20 Inspectors, 88 Sergeants and 895 Constables = ~1,013). The force grew toward an authorised establishment approaching 3,000 by early 1830, but was not 3,200 at launch. Stating '3,200' as the founding number overstates the initial establishment and could mislead exam candidates.
correction: The Metropolitan Police began with approximately 1,000 officers when it commenced patrols on 29 September 1829. The authorised establishment grew towards 3,000 by early 1830. The claim of '3,200 officers' at founding is not supported by primary sources.

lesson_title: Methods of punishment: medieval to early modern
claim: the theft of goods worth more than twelve pence (listed as an example of a Bloody Code capital offence, and again in the Key Fact box)
issue: The threshold for capital theft under the Bloody Code is commonly cited as goods worth more than one shilling (12 pence = 1 shilling). This figure itself is contested and varied by context (grand larceny was historically over 12d), so the claim is not strictly wrong, but the lesson states 'twelve pence' without noting this equals one shilling — which could cause student confusion. More significantly, the lesson lists this as the Bloody Code threshold, which is broadly defensible for grand larceny as it stood at certain periods. Minor issue of imprecision rather than a clear factual error.
correction: Theft of goods worth more than 12 pence (one shilling) was the historical grand larceny threshold. The lesson's figure is not wrong but noting '12 pence (one shilling)' would aid clarity for students.
source: Standard legal-history sources on the Bloody Code; threshold of grand larceny traditionally 12d = 1 shilling.

claim: Cholera first struck Britain in 1831–1832 and returned in 1848–1849 and 1853–1854.
issue: The third British cholera epidemic is conventionally dated 1853–1854, which is correct. However some authoritative sources date it 1853–1854 and others 1854 only (Snow's Broad Street investigation was 1854). The 1831–1832 and 1848–1849 dates are correct. No error here — this is accurate.
correction: No correction needed; dates are accurate and consistent with mainstream scholarship. Low flag only to note the third epidemic is sometimes cited as 1853–1854 or simply 1854.

claim: it had no public house until 1962, when the Skittles Inn (a non-alcoholic tavern) was replaced by a conventional pub only after a local referendum
issue: The Skittles Inn was NOT replaced by a pub in 1962. The Skittles Inn became the Settlement Adult Education Centre in 1925 — decades before the referendum. The first conventional licensed pub (the Broadway Hotel) opened in 1962 following a referendum held in 1957 (some sources say 1958). The Skittles Inn and the Broadway Hotel are separate buildings and events. The framing that the Skittles Inn was 'replaced' by a pub in 1962 conflates two unrelated events and is factually misleading.
correction: Letchworth had no conventional public house until the Broadway Hotel opened in 1962, following a local referendum (held c.1957–1958). The Skittles Inn was a temperance tavern that had become the Settlement Adult Education Centre in 1925 — it was not 'replaced' by the Broadway Hotel. These are separate buildings and separate events separated by nearly 40 years.

claim: Letchworth itself was eventually taken into community ownership in 1962 when the Letchworth Garden City Corporation purchased the town from its shareholders.
issue: The Letchworth Garden City Corporation did not 'purchase' the town from shareholders. Parliament passed the Letchworth Garden City Act 1962, which transferred the assets of First Garden City Ltd to a new statutory public corporation — this was a legislative compulsory transfer, not a market purchase. The trigger was that a private company (Hotel York Ltd) had been accumulating shares to take speculative control; Parliament intervened legislatively. The Corporation then formally took over on 1 January 1963 and paid agreed compensation of £3,115,000 to First Garden City Ltd. Saying 'purchased from shareholders' misstates the mechanism (it was a parliamentary forced transfer with compensation).
correction: In 1962 Parliament passed the Letchworth Garden City Act, creating the Letchworth Garden City Corporation as a statutory public body and transferring the estate to it (effective 1 January 1963). This was a legislative compulsory transfer prompted by fears of speculative private takeover, not a commercial purchase from shareholders. Compensation of £3,115,000 was paid to First Garden City Ltd.
